title: The CARM1 epigenetic enzyme inhibits cross-presenting dendritic cell function in cancer immunity.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed all small processed files from the five GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus) series. Counted: 3,127 KO-gained and 218 control-gained ATAC (assay for transposase-accessible chromatin) regions, all exactly 190 base pairs wide, all coordinates unique, spread over 20 chromosomes; 248,938 KO and 246,966 control called peaks (ENCODE narrowPeak format, median -log10 q-value ~21-23); 6,135 CARM1-HA protein-binding regions and 59,031 control vs 25,826 knockout H3R17me2 histone-mark peaks from CUT&RUN; RNA-seq tables of 35,949 genes x 6 samples (raw counts) and 17,521 genes x 10 samples (normalized). Confirmed genome build mm10 and the processing pipeline (Trim Galore, Bowtie2, MACS2) in every GEO sample record. Checked that all 3,127 KO-gained regions sit inside the deposited KO peak set. Cross-checked the gained regions against CARM1 binding and H3R17me2: they are depleted, not enriched (0.2% vs 0.8% background for CARM1 binding; 2.0% vs 22.5% for H3R17me2).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Nothing from the paper body: Science article is paywalled, there is no PubMed Central version, and science.org returns HTTP 403. Only the abstract (via Europe PMC and Crossref) and the GEO series summaries were readable. The claim that CARM1 inhibition opens chromatin at BATF3-Jun and RelA motif sites, the number of differentially accessible regions the authors report, and the exact statistical method used to define the 'KO-specific'/'control-specific' sets all come from the abstract or are simply unavailable.

a1_downloadable.note: Verified by downloading: five public GEO series (GSE300010/12/14/17/19), no login, no application. All processed files under 50 MB except two Seurat .RDS single-cell objects (370 MB and 51 MB), which the project does not need.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Borderline pass. For the binary task the label is file membership: a region is in GSE300010_ATAC_DC1_merged_KO_specific.bed (gained) or not. Background comes from one subtraction against the deposited peak set. A quantitative label (fold change per region) does NOT exist in any deposited file and could only be rebuilt from raw sequencing reads, which this project forbids.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs are DNA sequence. The files give mm10 coordinates, not sequence, but mm10 is a single reference download and extraction is mechanical (no per-item database lookups). Build is explicitly stated in every GEO sample record.

a4_units_stated.note: The label is categorical so needs no units. The narrowPeak files follow the documented ENCODE standard (signal value, -log10 p, -log10 q) and the pipeline is named. Weakness noted: the two 'specific' BED files carry only coordinates and a peak ID, with no effect size or significance column at all.

a5_enough_rows.note: Counted in the files: 3,127 KO-gained regions as positives, ~247,000 called peaks available as background, plus 6,135 CARM1-binding regions for an alternative task. Well over the ~400 needed for classification. The other direction is weak: only 218 control-gained regions.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~3 GB (2.6 GB uncompressed mm10 reference genome + ~15 MB of peak files)
a6_fits_laptop.note: All peak and count files together are ~16 MB. The only bulky item is the mouse reference genome, read by streaming index. A frozen-backbone baseline on ~20,000 short windows runs on CPU.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Internally consistent where checkable: all 3,127 KO-gained regions fall inside the deposited KO peak set, 0 duplicate coordinates anywhere, and the 26 RNA-seq GEO samples reconcile to 16 processed columns because 10 are re-sequencing runs merged with their partners (verified from sample titles). Cannot compare to the paper's own stated numbers: it is paywalled with no PubMed Central copy.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels come from MACS2 peak calls on real ATAC-seq reads, i.e. a physical measurement, not another model's output, and nothing about the label is computed from DNA sequence (the feature). Caveat: the differential call rests on 4 control vs 4 knockout samples and the deposited files contain no statistics, so the label cannot be re-derived or filtered by effect size.

B1.why: Five GEO series, but the four BED/narrowPeak files needed join cleanly on mm10 coordinates; verified.

B2.why: Every gzipped BED, narrowPeak and CSV parsed first try, no fixes; verified by opening all of them.

B3.why: One lab, one pipeline (Trim Galore, Bowtie2, MACS2, mm10) for all eight ATAC samples; read in GEO records.

B4.why: No censored or qualitative values; files contain coordinates and documented numeric peak statistics only.

B5.why: Counted zero duplicate coordinates: 3,127/3,127 and 218/218 unique, plus unique CUT&RUN peaks.

B6.why: narrowPeak is a documented standard, but the two 'specific' BED files have no stats column and no stated derivation.

C1.why: Cross-species transfer version is informative either way; within-dataset version just restates the paper's motif finding.

C2.why: ChromBPNet and gkm-SVM are open and strongly evaluated; WTKO-CNN (arXiv May 2026) does the exact task, code unknown.

C3.why: CARM1 in dendritic cells never modelled, but the generic knockout-versus-wildtype peak task has a 5-month-old precedent.

C4.why: ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN in primary mouse dendritic cells is slow, expensive wet-lab work.

C5.why: Obvious dummies available: GC content, AP-1 motif count, distance to transcription start site; ChromBPNet runnable.

D1.why: DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA are open-weight DNA language models matching 190-base-pair mm10 windows.

D2.why: ~20,000 short windows: embed once on CPU, cache, fit a linear head; no GPU needed.

D3.why: DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA permissively licensed; GEO data is public with no restrictions.

E1.why: Hold out whole chromosomes; 20 chromosomes present in the files, verified by counting.

E2.why: 20 chromosomes, each carrying dozens to hundreds of the 3,127 positives.

E3.why: Majority class, GC content and single AP-1 motif count are all computable dummies.

E4.why: No per-replicate signal deposited (all 8 ATAC samples list supplementary file NONE); noise floor unknowable.

E5.why: Abstract names BATF3-Jun and RelA motif enrichment the model must recover; a pre-specified literature control.

E6.why: Label shuffling and dinucleotide-shuffled sequence controls are trivial on this feature table.

E7.why: Independent human CARM1-perturbation chromatin data exists: GSE334083 (ATAC), GSE157117 (CUT&RUN), found in GEO.

E8.why: Paper paywalled with no PubMed Central copy, so no published number could be retrieved to reproduce.

G1.why: Standard mm10 genomic coordinates, build stated in every GEO sample record; verified.

G2.why: ImmGen ATAC, ChIP-Atlas mouse TF ChIP-seq and ENCODE mouse cCREs all join on mm10 coordinates.

G3.why: Coordinate overlap is one-to-many; needs an explicit collapse rule per region.

G4.why: Asks whether CARM1-restrained elements are cDC1-specific enhancers or generic AP-1 sites open everywhere.

H1.why: Both directions present but wildly asymmetric (3,127 gained vs 218 lost) and no effect sizes; counted in files.

H2.why: One lab, one species, one cell type: mouse bone-marrow-derived type 1 conventional dendritic cells.

H3.why: The honest claim can be stated precisely in one sentence; see honest_claim_h3.

H4.why: Alignment and peak calling documented in GEO; the differential-call method is not, and the paper is paywalled.

I1.why: Wucherpfennig lab at Dana-Farber, plus developers of the CARM1 inhibitor EZM2302 (Epizyme/Ipsen).

I2.why: Could prioritise reporter assays on candidate enhancers, but nobody is currently waiting on this prediction.

I3.why: Precision among a top-100 shortlist matches 'which regions to test'; ranking metrics only roughly aligned.

I4.why: A motif-count logistic regression may match a DNA language model; that is the main risk, untested here.

J1.why: Real transfer learning, chromosome-held-out splits, interpretability and a cross-species validation set.

J2.why: AP-1 and NF-kB motif recovery gives a clear, pre-specified way to tell sense from nonsense.

J3.why: A curated CARM1-responsive-element benchmark plus motif baseline is shareable even if the deep model fails.

J4.why: No budget stated by the data; three weeks is a reasonable proposal but not yet committed.

J5.why: A kill condition is proposable (motif baseline matches the model) but is not written down anywhere yet.

existing_models.name: WTKO-CNN (arXiv 2605.24034, May 2026), a convolutional neural network with attention that classifies DNA sequences as wild-type-specific or knockout-specific ATAC peaks
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrievable: the arXiv abstract page gives no accuracy or area-under-curve numbers and does not state the train/test split. Evaluated on three mouse chromatin accessibility datasets (RelA, LSD1, Ebf1 perturbations).
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not stated on the abstract page; the framing emphasises interpretability (saliency-guided k-mer extraction, motif discovery) over generalisation.

existing_models.name: ChromBPNet (Kundaje lab), a bias-corrected convolutional model predicting base-resolution chromatin accessibility from DNA sequence
existing_models.score_and_split: Published as competitive with much larger models at predicting variant effects on accessibility, pioneer transcription factor binding and reporter activity across cell contexts; trained and evaluated per cell type with held-out chromosomes. Exact numbers not retrieved here.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Separating true regulatory sequence signal from assay enzyme bias, and transferring across cell contexts, are the problems the method is built around.

existing_models.name: gkm-SVM / lsgkm, gapped k-mer support vector machines for regulatory sequence classification
existing_models.score_and_split: Long-standing open baseline for exactly this kind of positive-versus-background regulatory sequence classification; numbers depend on dataset, none retrieved for CARM1.

backbone.name: DNABERT-2 or HyenaDNA (open-weight DNA language models on HuggingFace), with gkm-SVM and a motif-count logistic regression as the non-neural comparators
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU, 16 GB RAM. Embed ~20,000 windows of 190-1,000 base pairs once, cache them, then fit a linear or gradient-boosted head.
backbone.licence: DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA are permissively licensed and downloadable; GEO data carries no use restriction.

integration.partner_dataset: ImmGen ATAC (open chromatin across dozens of mouse immune cell types) and ChIP-Atlas (thousands of mouse transcription-factor ChIP-seq peak sets, including BATF3, IRF8 and RelA), with ENCODE mouse candidate cis-regulatory elements as a third layer
integration.join_key: mm10 genomic coordinates (build stated in every GEO sample record), by interval overlap
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Are the regulatory elements that CARM1 holds shut a dendritic-cell-specific set of BATF3/IRF8 enhancers, or generic AP-1 elements that are already open in many other immune cell types?

controls.positive_control: Two, both pre-specified: (1) predict GC content or sequence length from the window as a plumbing check, which must be near-perfect; (2) the model's learned features must recover AP-1/BATF3-Jun and NF-kB/RelA motifs, which the paper's abstract names as the enriched motifs in regions opened by CARM1 inhibition.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the gained/background labels and confirm performance collapses to the majority-class dummy; replace sequences with dinucleotide-preserving shuffles; shuffle labels within chromosome to confirm the grouped split is actually grouping.
controls.external_validation: Independent human CARM1-perturbation chromatin datasets found in GEO: GSE334083 (ATAC-seq, 9 samples, human, arginine methylation of BAF155) and GSE157117 (CUT&RUN, 8 samples, human ovarian cancer CARM1). Different species and cell type, so this tests transfer rather than replication.

honest_claim_h3: Among chromatin regions that are already accessible in mouse bone-marrow-derived type 1 conventional dendritic cells from one lab, local DNA sequence predicts which ones gain accessibility when CARM1 is deleted, to the extent captured by a 4-versus-4 replicate differential peak call with no deposited effect sizes.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use local DNA sequence to predict which already-open regulatory regions open further when the CARM1 enzyme is removed from dendritic cells.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example is one 190-base-pair stretch of the mouse genome (build mm10) that is an open-chromatin region in dendritic cells. Verified counts: 3,127 regions that gained accessibility after CARM1 deletion, 218 that lost it, and ~247,000 other open regions available as background.
plain_idea.predict: A probability that the region gains accessibility when CARM1 is gone. The true answer comes from ATAC-seq, a lab assay that cuts DNA wherever chromatin is loose, run on 4 control and 4 CARM1-knockout mouse dendritic cell samples and compared by the original authors.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Companies developing CARM1 inhibitors as cancer immunotherapy would get a ranked shortlist of which immune-gene enhancers the drug actually opens, to test in reporter assays. Even if the model fails, we learn whether the response to an epigenetic drug is written in local sequence at all, or is purely contextual.

more_or_better_data.why: 3,127 positive regions from one mouse cell type is small next to what ChromBPNet and gkm-SVM are trained on (hundreds of thousands of peaks per cell type across many ENCODE cell contexts). The only distinctive thing is the perturbation (CARM1, an arginine methyltransferase), not the scale.

confidence_score.why: No per-replicate signal was deposited: all eight ATAC samples list supplementary file NONE, and the differential BED files carry no p-value or fold change. Without replicate-level measurements there is no way to estimate measurement noise and therefore no basis for a calibrated per-region confidence.

models_beatable.why: WTKO-CNN is a May 2026 arXiv preprint with no retrievable split details, metrics or code, so re-doing its task honestly on held-out chromosomes is legitimate. ChromBPNet (2024-2025, open, chromosome-held-out evaluation, bias-corrected) is not beatable at accessibility prediction and should be used as a baseline rather than a target.

guaranteed_improvement.why: The proposed partner data (human CARM1 ATAC GSE334083, ImmGen mouse immune ATAC) is from different labs, species or cell types and measures accessibility in a different context, so condition three fails: it is not the same quantity measured the same way. It would also require a different evaluation split.

label_elsewhere.sources: GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus) holds many wild-type-versus-knockout ATAC-seq comparisons, three of which the WTKO-CNN preprint used (RelA, LSD1, Ebf1). For CARM1 specifically I found GSE334083 (human ATAC with arginine-methylation perturbation), GSE157117 and GSE95645 (human CARM1 CUT&RUN) by searching GEO. ChIP-Atlas and ENCODE/ImmGen hold baseline accessibility but not perturbation responses.
label_elsewhere.join_key: Genomic coordinates plus genome build (mm10 here, hg38 for the human sets); cross-species joins need liftover or orthology, so the practical join is in motif/sequence space rather than coordinates.
label_elsewhere.why: A handful of other perturbation datasets means a real external test of whether sequence determinants of epigenetic-drug response transfer, but they are small, scattered and need per-dataset reprocessing rather than a single lookup.

risks: Neighbouring open-chromatin regions a few kilobases apart share sequence context and regulatory identity, so a random split would put near-duplicate regions in both training and test.

Gained regions are strongly depleted for the promoter-associated H3R17me2 mark (2.0% overlap versus 22.5% for random control peaks, measured here), so the model could simply learn 'distal enhancer versus CpG-rich promoter', i.e. GC content, and look accurate for the wrong reason.
Background regions drawn from the same pooled peak file as the positives inherit the same sequencing depth and Tn5 enzyme cut-site bias, which a sequence model can pick up as a technical shortcut.
Repeat elements and segmental duplications place literally identical sequence in multiple genomic locations, which can straddle the split.
The label comes from only 4 versus 4 samples with no deposited statistics, so an unknown fraction of the 3,127 'gained' regions are false positives that no split can fix.
leakage_plan.split: Hold out whole chromosomes (leave-chromosome-out, 20 folds). The grouping column is the first column of the BED files, which I opened and confirmed contains 20 distinct chromosomes for both the gained and lost sets. Additionally match background regions to positives on GC content and distance to the nearest transcription start site before splitting, so the model cannot win on promoter architecture alone.
checks: Shuffle the gained/background labels and confirm the area under the precision-recall curve collapses to the positive-class prevalence.

Train on GC content alone, and separately on distance to the nearest transcription start site alone, and report those numbers next to the full model; if either is close, the model has learned promoter architecture, not CARM1 biology.
Compute nearest-neighbour sequence similarity between each held-out region and the training set, and drop test regions within 10 kilobases of any training region.
Replace real sequences with dinucleotide-preserving shuffles and confirm the model drops to the dummy.
leakage_plan.verdict: Manageable but genuinely risky: chromosome-held-out splitting is easy, but the GC/promoter confound is large (an 11-fold depletion of a promoter mark measured directly in the files) and must be controlled by matched background selection or the whole result is an artifact.

success_criteria.metric: Precision among the top 100 ranked regions under leave-one-chromosome-out cross-validation, because the realistic use is handing a wet lab a shortlist of candidate enhancers to test in a reporter assay. Report area under the precision-recall curve alongside it.
success_criteria.baselines: Three, all computable here: (1) positive-class prevalence as the trivial dummy (3,127 out of ~247,000 peaks, i.e. ~1.3%, if all called peaks are background); (2) a single AP-1 motif count feature in logistic regression; (3) gkm-SVM, an open gapped k-mer support vector machine. No published number exists for this dataset, since the paper is paywalled and its motif analysis is an enrichment test, not a predictive model.
success_criteria.success: The frozen DNA language model beats the AP-1-motif-count logistic regression by at least 10 precision points in the top 100 on GC-matched background and leave-one-chromosome-out splits, AND its learned features independently recover both AP-1/BATF3-Jun and NF-kB/RelA motifs.
success_criteria.kill: The AP-1 motif count alone matches the deep model within 5 precision points in the top 100, or GC content alone reaches an area under the precision-recall curve within 20% of the full model. Either outcome means the project is a one-page note, and both are checkable in under a day.

ambitious.why: Publishes sequence-to-regulatory-activity methods with biological payoff; would need the model to clearly beat motif and gkm-SVM baselines AND transfer to the independent human CARM1 datasets, showing that epigenetic-drug response is sequence-encoded across species.

realistic.why: The likely result is a careful, honestly split benchmark showing a DNA language model gives a modest gain over motif counts on one perturbation dataset, with the GC/promoter confound quantified; that is exactly an Applications Note or short methods paper.

fallback.journal: NAR Genomics and Bioinformatics, or a bioRxiv preprint plus a machine-learning-in-computational-biology workshop
fallback.why: Publishes negative and partial results; a paper reporting that AP-1 motif content explains most CARM1-responsive accessibility and that language-model embeddings add nothing is still a useful, citable warning to this subfield.

pitch.headline: 3,127 verified mouse regulatory regions that open when a druggable epigenetic enzyme is removed, with the enriched motifs named in advance as a positive control.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: CARM1 is an arginine methyltransferase with a clinical-stage inhibitor (EZM2302); its accessibility response has never been modelled. Three assays in one mouse cell type: 8 ATAC samples, 6,135 CARM1 binding regions, 59,031 control H3R17me2 peaks. All opened and counted.
pitch.the_win: Beat an AP-1-motif-count logistic regression by 10 or more precision points in the top 100 under leave-one-chromosome-out splits, and have the model's features independently rediscover BATF3-Jun and RelA motifs.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: We learn whether response to an epigenetic drug is written in local DNA sequence at all. I already measured a likely spoiler: gained regions are 11-fold depleted for the promoter mark H3R17me2 (2.0% vs 22.5%), so GC content may explain everything.
pitch.who_wants_it: The Wucherpfennig lab at Dana-Farber and developers of CARM1 inhibitors (EZM2302, Epizyme/Ipsen), who would get a ranked shortlist of immune-gene enhancers to test in reporter assays.

ml_idea: Binary classification from DNA sequence: given a 190-base-pair (optionally widened to 1 kilobase) mm10 window that is an open-chromatin region in mouse type 1 conventional dendritic cells, predict whether it gains accessibility when CARM1 is deleted. Positives are the 3,127 deposited KO-gained regions; negatives are GC- and promoter-distance-matched regions drawn from the ~247,000 called peaks. Features are frozen DNABERT-2 or HyenaDNA embeddings, cached once on CPU, with a linear or gradient-boosted head; comparators are an AP-1/NF-kB motif-count logistic regression and gkm-SVM. Evaluation is leave-one-chromosome-out (20 folds), with external transfer tested on the independent human CARM1 chromatin datasets GSE334083 and GSE157117. A second, less crowded variant worth trying: predict the 6,135 CARM1-HA binding regions from sequence, which asks which transcription factor motifs recruit a coactivator that has no DNA-binding domain of its own.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed. Peak files total ~16 MB (measured by download). The mm10 reference is ~2.6 GB uncompressed and is read through a streaming index, so RAM stays low. Embedding time assumes ~20,000 short windows at a few windows per second on a laptop CPU; the 20-fold chromosome cross-validation is a linear head on a cached 20,000 x 768 matrix, which is seconds to minutes.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Extract mm10 sequence for the 3,127 gained regions and a GC-matched background, then count AP-1 (TGASTCA) matches in each. If that single feature already separates them with area under the precision-recall curve above ~0.6, the deep model has almost nothing left to add and the project is a one-page note. This is one afternoon and must be done before anything else.

verdict_reason: Everything in Part A passes and I verified it in the files: 3,127 gained and 218 lost 190-base-pair regions, zero duplicates, 20 chromosomes, mm10 stated, ~247,000 background peaks, all downloading freely in ~16 MB. Model-readiness is good (10/12) and the backbone fit is perfect (6/6). What holds it back is the question, not the data. The exact task (classify wild-type versus knockout ATAC peaks from sequence) already has a May 2026 preprint, WTKO-CNN, and the surrounding field has ChromBPNet and gkm-SVM, both open and honestly evaluated. The authors deposited no per-replicate signal and no effect sizes (all eight ATAC samples list supplementary file NONE), so there is no quantitative label, no noise floor, and no way to filter weak differential calls. Most damning, I measured a confound directly: the gained regions are 11-fold depleted for the promoter-associated H3R17me2 mark (2.0% overlap versus 22.5% for random control peaks) and almost never overlap CARM1's own binding sites (0.2% versus 0.8%), so a sequence model here is at serious risk of learning 'distal enhancer versus promoter' and the likely honest result is that AP-1 motif content, which the paper already reported, explains most of it. Park it: a clean, cheap weekend project with real learning value and a sharp one-day kill check, but low impact and one lab, one species, one cell type.
